title: Frontier Reasoning Reaches the Edge: How to Deploy and Optimize Models on NVIDIA Jetson | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA shows that compact 2026-era open reasoning models (Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, Qwen3.8-27B) now match 2025 frontier-model intelligence scores at a fraction of the parameter count, and that combining NVFP4 quantization with speculative decoding delivers up to a 6.28x decode-throughput speedup on Jetson edge hardware versus BF16, letting agentic reasoning run locally without a data-center round trip.

themes.theme: Edge AI capability shift: frontier reasoning without the data center

insights.claim: Until recently, models capable of multi-step reasoning were too large to run locally on edge hardware, forcing developers to route inference through a data center, which added network dependency, increased costs, and exposed data that may have needed to stay on-device.
insights.speaker: Khalil BenKhaled
insights.so_what: Names the specific cost, latency, and data-privacy penalties of cloud-dependent edge AI that the new generation of compact models is designed to eliminate.
insights.quote: Developers building agents have had to route inference through a data center, adding network dependency, increasing costs, and exposing data that may need to stay on device.
insights.locator: Running reasoning and agentic AI at the edge has been harder than it needs to be.

insights.claim: According to the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index plotted by model size and release date, open models released in 2026 now reach intelligence scores similar to leading 2025 models while using far fewer parameters.
insights.speaker: Khalil BenKhaled
insights.so_what: A cross-vendor intelligence-per-parameter benchmark shows a real efficiency frontier shift, not just an NVIDIA-specific claim, supporting the broader thesis that edge deployment of reasoning models is now economically viable.
insights.quote: Open models released in 2026 now reach scores similar to leading models from 2025, while using far fewer parameters.

insights.claim: Running agent reasoning loops locally on Jetson next to sensors and systems enables use cases such as in-cab assistants, real-time anomaly detection, and robots operating in harsh or remote environments where connectivity is limited or unavailable.
insights.speaker: Khalil BenKhaled
insights.so_what: Identifies concrete commercial application categories (industrial, automotive, robotics) that become newly addressable once frontier-grade reasoning fits on edge hardware, expanding NVIDIA Jetson's total addressable market.
insights.quote: This could power in-cab assistants, real-time anomaly detection, and robots working in harsh or remote environments.
insights.locator: Running reasoning and agentic AI at the edge has been harder than it needs to be.

themes.theme: Model architecture tradeoffs: MoE vs. dense for agent workloads

insights.claim: Qwen3.8-27B is a dense model that activates all 27 billion parameters for every token, while Nemotron 3.5 Lightning uses a mixture-of-experts architecture with 30 billion total parameters but activates only 3 billion parameters per token.
insights.speaker: Khalil BenKhaled
insights.so_what: The tenfold difference in active parameters per token between a similarly 'sized' dense model and an MoE model directly drives which one is cheaper and faster to run on constrained edge hardware.
insights.quote: It has 30 billion total parameters but activates only 3 billion for each token.
insights.locator: How do you choose a reasoning model for Jetson?

insights.claim: Nemotron 3.5 Lightning was distilled from the larger Nemotron 3 Ultra model, transferring some of the larger model's capabilities into a form small enough to run on edge hardware.
insights.speaker: Khalil BenKhaled
insights.so_what: Distillation from a data-center-scale model is the specific technique enabling frontier capability to reach edge-sized models, a repeatable playbook for shrinking future frontier models.
insights.quote: distillation transfers some of Nemotron 3 Ultra's capabilities into the smaller Nemotron 3.5 Lightning model
insights.locator: How do you choose a reasoning model for Jetson?

insights.claim: Nemotron 3.5 Lightning's mixture-of-experts architecture suits response-heavy agent workflows where faster token generation shortens the overall process, while Qwen3.8-27B's dense architecture suits tasks requiring fewer but harder decisions where the agent can spend more time generating each response.
insights.speaker: Khalil BenKhaled
insights.so_what: Gives developers a concrete decision framework for matching model architecture to agent workload shape rather than picking a model on parameter count alone.
insights.quote: Nemotron 3.5 Lightning is a good fit for these response-heavy workflows, where faster token generation can shorten the overall process. Qwen3.8-27B is a better fit for tasks that require fewer, harder decisions
insights.locator: How do you choose a reasoning model for Jetson?

insights.claim: Gemma 4 E4B is recommended as a strong starting point for the smaller Jetson Orin Nano, while Nemotron 3.5 Lightning and Qwen3.8-27B are recommended for the more capable Jetson AGX Orin and Jetson AGX Thor.
insights.speaker: Khalil BenKhaled
insights.so_what: Maps specific model choices to specific Jetson hardware tiers, giving buyers a concrete product-fit guide across NVIDIA's edge hardware line.
insights.quote: Gemma 4 E4B is a strong starting point for Jetson Orin Nano. For Jetson AGX Orin and Jetson AGX Thor, Nemotron 3.5 Lightning and Qwen3.8-27B are strong options.
insights.locator: How do you choose a reasoning model for Jetson?

themes.theme: Quantization and speculative decoding performance gains

insights.claim: Combining NVFP4 quantization with the fastest tested speculative decoding configuration for each model delivers up to a 6.28x decode throughput speedup on Jetson compared with BF16.
insights.speaker: Khalil BenKhaled
insights.so_what: A 6.28x throughput gain from software-level optimization alone (no new hardware) materially lowers the effective cost and latency of running reasoning models at the edge, improving unit economics for edge AI deployments.
insights.quote: NVFP4 quantization and speculative decoding together deliver up to 6.28x decode throughput speedup over BF16 on Jetson
insights.locator: How do you optimize reasoning-model inference on Jetson?

insights.claim: NVFP4 quantization reduces the amount of data the GPU must move and process during each decoding pass, improving generation speed and reducing memory use while keeping output quality close to BF16.
insights.speaker: Khalil BenKhaled
insights.so_what: Lower-precision inference is a key lever for fitting larger, more capable models into the memory and compute budget of edge devices without materially sacrificing quality.
insights.quote: With a format such as NVFP4, you can improve generation speed and reduce memory use while keeping quality close to BF16.
insights.locator: How do you optimize reasoning-model inference on Jetson?

insights.claim: Speculative decoding uses a smaller draft model to propose several tokens at once, which the main model verifies together; if several proposed tokens are accepted, generation advances by multiple tokens in a single verification step instead of one token per full model pass.
insights.speaker: Khalil BenKhaled
insights.so_what: Explains the mechanism behind a major inference-acceleration technique that is model-architecture agnostic and increasingly standard across the industry for reducing serving costs.
insights.quote: A smaller draft model proposes several tokens, and the main model verifies them together.
insights.locator: How do you optimize reasoning-model inference on Jetson?

insights.claim: NVFP4 quantization and speculative decoding are complementary optimizations: quantization reduces the cost of each inference pass while speculative decoding increases the number of accepted tokens produced per pass, so combining them improves performance more than either technique alone.
insights.speaker: Khalil BenKhaled
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that stacking orthogonal optimization techniques compounds performance gains, a reusable principle for anyone optimizing LLM inference cost on constrained hardware.
insights.quote: The two optimizations complement each other. NVFP4 reduces the cost of each pass, while speculative decoding increases the number of accepted tokens produced from each pass.
insights.locator: How do you optimize reasoning-model inference on Jetson?

themes.theme: Speculative decoding method selection is model-specific

insights.claim: The fastest speculative decoding configuration differs by model: Nemotron 3.5 Lightning performed best with DSpark, while Qwen3.8-27B performed best with DFlash2, so developers should test methods and draft checkpoints against their specific target model rather than assuming one configuration works universally.
insights.speaker: Khalil BenKhaled
insights.so_what: Warns against generalizing a single 'best' optimization recipe across models, which affects how engineering teams should budget testing time before deployment.
insights.quote: Nemotron 3.5 Lightning performed best with DSpark, while Qwen3.8-27B performed best with DFlash2.
insights.locator: How do you optimize reasoning-model inference on Jetson?

insights.claim: Three speculative decoding draft methods run on Jetson with different tradeoffs: MTP uses prediction heads trained with the main model across mainstream families like Qwen, Gemma, and Nemotron; DFlash uses a separate diffusion-based draft model and supports the widest range of compatible checkpoints; DSpark builds on DFlash by correcting drafts and stopping weak proposals early, and can be faster but supports fewer checkpoints.
insights.speaker: Khalil BenKhaled
insights.so_what: Gives developers a decision matrix for choosing among competing speculative decoding methods based on checkpoint availability versus raw speed.
insights.quote: DSpark can be faster when a matching checkpoint is available, but it supports fewer checkpoints.
insights.locator: Each method creates and evaluates draft tokens differently, which affects the cost and accuracy of its proposals.

insights.claim: Testing four SpeedBench categories (writing, reasoning, summarization, and retrieval-augmented generation) with each model's fastest configuration held fixed showed that the same method remained fastest across categories for a given model, but raw throughput still varied substantially by workload type, with RAG and writing benefiting the most.
insights.speaker: Khalil BenKhaled
insights.so_what: Shows that a single throughput number from a model-level benchmark can mask large workload-specific variance, meaning production throughput estimates must be validated per use case rather than assumed from a generic benchmark.
insights.quote: Speculative decoding speedup varied by workload, with RAG and writing benefiting most for both models

insights.claim: Across the tested SpeedBench workload categories, Nemotron 3.5 Lightning with DSpark ranged from 123.01 to 138.02 output tokens per second, while Qwen3.8-27B with DFlash2 ranged from 27.69 to 34.44 output tokens per second.
insights.speaker: Khalil BenKhaled
insights.so_what: Nemotron 3.5 Lightning's MoE architecture delivers roughly 4x higher raw output throughput than the dense Qwen3.8-27B on the same edge hardware, a concrete data point for capacity planning and cost-per-token comparisons.
insights.quote: Nemotron 3.5 Lightning with DSpark ranged from 123.01 to 138.02 output tokens/s, while Qwen3.8-27B with DFlash2 ranged from 27.69 to 34.44 output tokens/s.

insights.claim: General benchmarks cannot confirm whether a specific quantized or speculative-decoding checkpoint preserves the behavior that matters for an application's own data, so developers should test configurations with prompts representative of their intended application before deploying.
insights.speaker: Khalil BenKhaled
insights.so_what: A direct caution against relying solely on published benchmark numbers when selecting a production inference configuration, since accuracy and acceleration are workload-dependent.
insights.quote: General benchmarks cannot tell you whether a checkpoint preserves the behavior that matters for your data.
insights.locator: When should you train a custom checkpoint?

themes.theme: When to invest in custom checkpoint training

insights.claim: Most applications should start with an existing quantized checkpoint and draft model, since that is usually enough to achieve strong accuracy and a useful speedup without training anything custom; teams should only train their own checkpoints when testing reveals a clear performance or accuracy gap.
insights.speaker: Khalil BenKhaled
insights.so_what: Sets a practical cost-benefit default for engineering teams: avoid the expense of custom model training unless off-the-shelf checkpoints demonstrably underperform for the specific use case.
insights.quote: Most applications will not need custom training. Start with the available checkpoints, measure their accuracy and performance, and train your own only when those results show a clear gap.
insights.locator: When should you train a custom checkpoint?

insights.claim: If quantization reduces accuracy, NVIDIA Model Optimizer can fine-tune the quantized model using quantization-aware training (which simulates lower precision during training) or quantization-aware distillation (which additionally uses a higher-precision teacher model to help the quantized model retain the original model's behavior).
insights.speaker: Khalil BenKhaled
insights.so_what: Provides a concrete remediation path when quantization degrades accuracy, reducing the risk that teams abandon quantization gains entirely due to quality concerns.
insights.quote: If quantization reduces accuracy, use NVIDIA Model Optimizer to fine-tune the quantized model with quantization-aware training or distillation.
insights.locator: When should you train a custom checkpoint?

insights.claim: When a public speculative-decoding draft checkpoint provides less acceleration than expected because the main model has a low acceptance rate for its proposed tokens, developers can use the vLLM Speculators training guide (supporting MTP, EAGLE-3, DFlash, and DSpark) to train a compatible speculator using their own representative application data.
insights.speaker: Khalil BenKhaled
insights.so_what: Identifies token-acceptance rate as the key metric that determines whether speculative decoding delivers real acceleration, and gives a fallback path (custom speculator training) when a public checkpoint underperforms.
insights.quote: When the acceptance rate is low, the cost of producing and verifying drafts can reduce the benefit.
insights.locator: When should you train a custom checkpoint?
